questions.knowledge_point: Finding Where the Extrema of a Quadratic Form Are Attained on the Unit Sphere
questions.problem: The minimum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=-{x}_{1}^{2}-17{x}_{2}^{2}+7{x}_{3}^{2}-18{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $-20.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -17 & -9 \\ 0 & -9 & 7\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-20:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-20)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -17 & -9 \\ 0 & -9 & 7\end{aligned}]+20[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}19 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 \\ 0 & -9 & 27\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-20)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ 

Finally, dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem: The maximum value of the quadratic form $Q(x)=2{x}_{1}^{2}-{x}_{2}^{2}-{x}_{3}^{2}-2{x}_{2}{x}_{3},$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to $2.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the maximum is attained?
questions.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the matrix corresponding to our quadratic form. Recall that: 

- The maximum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the largest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
max{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{max}}
$$

 
The maximum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{max}}.$

- The minimum value of $Q(x),$ when $‖x‖=1,$ is equal to the smallest eigenvalue of $A:$

$$
min{Q(x)\,|\,‖x‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}
$$

 
The minimum is attained on the corresponding unit eigenvector ${u}_{\text{min}}.$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Now, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{max}}=2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & -1\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ 

Therefore,

$$
{u}_{\text{max}}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Where the Extrema of a Quadratic Form Is Attained Over an Ellipse
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=2$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=3$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{3},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinates matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18 & -4 \\ -6 & -12\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -12 \\ -12 & 36\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we maximize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual. Calculating the eigenvalues $B,$ we obtain the following:   

$$
\begin{aligned}|B-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}36-\lambda  & -12 \\ -12 & 36-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (36-\lambda )(36-\lambda )-144 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-72\lambda +1\,152 & =0 \\ (\lambda -48)(\lambda -24) & =0 \\ \lambda  & =48,\,24\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
min{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{\text{min}}=24.
$$

questions.problem: The minimum value of $Q(x)=8{x}_{1}^{2}-30{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-50{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+25{x}_{2}^{2}=100,$ is $-250.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=5$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{5}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}8 & -15 \\ -15 & -50\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}40 & -75 \\ -30 & -100\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-250,$ we have

$$
min{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{min}=-250.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-250:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-250I) & =[\begin{aligned}200 & -150 \\ -150 & -200\end{aligned}]+250[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}450 & -150 \\ -150 & 50\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-250I))y=0$ gives the eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{10},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: The minimum value of $Q(x)=4{x}_{1}^{2}-36{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2},$ when $4{x}_{1}^{2}+9{x}_{2}^{2}=36,$ is $-72.$ Which of the following is a vector $x$ at which the minimum is attained?
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that we can write the constraint equation as follows:

$$
\frac{{x}_{1}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{x}_{2}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $a=3$ (along the ${x}_{1}$-axis) and $b=2$ (along the ${x}_{2}$-axis). If we introduce new variables

$\,$ ${y}_{1}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{3}\,$ and $\,{y}_{2}=\frac{{x}_{2}}{2},$

the equation of the ellipse will transform into ${y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}=1$ or $‖y‖=1.$

So, introducing a change-of-coordinate matrix 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],
$$

 

we obtain that $x=Py.$ Substituting this into the expression of the quadratic form, we get

$$
Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax=(Py)^{T}A\,(Py)={y}^{T}\,({P}^{T}AP)y={Q}^{′}(y).
$$

As a result, since ${P}^{T}=P,$ the matrix of our quadratic form in new coordinates is 

$$
\begin{aligned}B & ={P}^{T}\,AP \\  & =PAP \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -18 \\ -18 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -54 \\ -36 & 18\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we minimize ${Q}^{′}(y)$ when $‖y‖=1,$ as usual.

Since we are told that the minimum value of the quadratic form is $-72,$ we have

$$
min{{Q}^{′}(y)\,|\,‖y‖=1}={\lambda }_{min}=-72.
$$

Next, we need the unit eigenvector that corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{\text{min}}=-72:$

$$
\begin{aligned}B-(-72)I & =[\begin{aligned}36 & -108 \\ -108 & 36\end{aligned}]+72[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}108 & -108 \\ -108 & 108\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(B-(-72)I)x=0$ gives the  eigenvector $v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing $v$ by its norm $‖v‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
{u}_{\text{min}}=\frac{v}{‖v‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Finally, we map this vector back to the initial coordinate  system using the change-of-coordinates matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{\text{min}} & =P{u}_{\text{min}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
